::: {#hero}

::: {.lead}
Associate Professor of Data Science and MBA programmes at the [Madras School of Economics](https://mse.ac.in), Chennai. I work on applied natural language processing and transformer-based models, predictive modelling in financial market microstructure and cross-market connectedness, and on generative AI in management, education and social science - after a decade in industry as Lead Data Scientist at PwC and in payments software as SME Developer at RS Software.
:::

I teach in the M.Sc. Data Science and MBA programmes at MSE. Before that I was Assistant Professor and Chairperson of Information Management & Analytics at IMI Bhubaneswar (where I also chaired IT Infrastructure & Cybersecurity and served as Associate Editor of the *IMIB Journal of Innovation & Management*, Sage), Assistant Professor of IT Systems & Analytics at IIM Bodh Gaya, Assistant Professor of Data Science at IFMR GSB, Krea University, and Assistant Professor and Chairperson of Business Analytics at IMT Ghaziabad. My PhD is from IIT Kharagpur, on predictive analytics in high-frequency market microstructure.

:::

## Education

**Ph.D. in Business Analytics**, Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, 2014–2017 (full-time, MHRD scholarship)
: *Thesis:* Determinants of Bid-Ask Spread and its Implications on Execution Probability in High Frequency Trading.
: Research on market microstructure explores how the working processes of a market affect prices, transaction costs, trading volume and trading behaviour. The availability of high-frequency orders-and-quotes data has let the classic theories, built on low-frequency data, be re-examined. The thesis empirically analyses, under Indian conditions, (a) the factors driving bid-ask spread, (b) asymmetric-information and transaction costs embedded in the spread, and (c) limit-order execution probability and hazard rates. Return volatility, share price, trading volume and number of trades are significant determinants of spreads; order-processing cost rises with volume; volatility and volume raise the asymmetric-information cost; same-side book depth, opposite-side open indicator, remaining time intervals, spread and tick volume determine execution probability; and tick volume, remaining intervals, quoted spread, price aggressiveness, book depth, return volatility and inferior price drive survival. The findings carry implications for traders and for the exchange regulator.
: *Keywords:* market microstructure, limit order book, order-processing cost, asymmetric-information cost, execution probability, hazard rates, survival analysis.

**M.Tech. in Soft Computing (Information Technology)**, Indian Institute of Engineering Science and Technology (IIEST), Shibpur, 2012
: *Thesis:* Design and FPGA-based implementation of a MUX/DEMUX system in SONET/SDH data communication networks.

**B.E. in Computer Science and Technology**, IIEST Shibpur, 2008
